title: Process death & state restoration
scopeHtml: Why and when the OS kills your process, what survives, how saved state really flows to system_server and back, and how to test it.

notes.title: Why the OS kills processes
notes.html:
The idea, simply. A phone has limited memory, and many apps want to run. When memory gets tight, Android quietly closes the apps you are not looking at to make room, like a waiter clearing plates nobody is eating from. Your app gets no warning and no chance to say goodbye. When the user comes back, Android restarts the app and expects it to look as if nothing happened. That is process death, and handling it is what separates a toy app from a production app.

Mechanism.

  • Every app runs in a Linux process. Android ranks processes by importance (oom_adj / "process state"): foreground (the activity the user is looking at, or a foreground service), visible, perceptible (e.g., music), service, cached (a stopped activity with no active components), and empty. The kernel-side daemon lmkd (low memory killer daemon, using PSI "pressure stall information" since Android 10) kills the least important processes first when memory pressure rises. ActivityManagerService also has ProcessList and a cap on cached processes.
  • Typical killers: low memory (most common while the app is in the background), user "Force stop" in settings, swipe-away from recents on some OEMs, battery-saver/OEM task killers (Xiaomi, Oppo, Vivo, Samsung "sleeping apps"), adb shell am kill, app update/install, permission revoked in settings (see below), crash/ANR, and "developer options: Don't keep activities" (which destroys activities, not the process).
  • A stopped (background) activity is free to be killed: the system guarantees onSaveInstanceState was called (before or after onStop, see below), but not onDestroy.
  • Cached processes: Android 12+ also freezes them (cached apps freezer), and Android 14 more aggressively; Android 15 adds app-process "stopped state" for apps force-stopped.

Swipe-away vs system kill vs finish (Q71).

Event Saved instance state kept? onDestroy called? Task restored on return?
User presses Back/finish() No (activity gone for good) Yes (isFinishing true) New task starts clean
System kills background process Yes (the system keeps the saved Bundle with the task record) No Yes: activity recreated with the Bundle
User swipes app from Recents Usually No (task removed, saved state discarded) Not reliably Fresh launch
Force stop in Settings No No Fresh launch
Config change Yes Yes (isChangingConfigurations) Same task

The important point: system kill keeps the task's saved state, swipe-away and force stop do not. So a test for "restore" must use the system-kill path, and a user who swipes away will see a fresh app; apps must persist anything that should survive that (a draft) in durable storage.

Industry examples. Low-end device fleets (Indian market, 2 to 3 GB RAM) see process death constantly for WhatsApp, Instagram and banking apps while the user switches to the camera or UPI; Xiaomi/Oppo "aggressive" killers cause notification issues documented by dontkillmyapp.com.

Everyday analogy. A hotel that needs rooms: it quietly clears the room of the guest who has been out longest, stores their bag at the desk (saved state), and gives it back if they return. If the guest officially checks out (finish) or the guest throws the bag away (swipe), nothing is stored.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying onDestroy is called when the OS kills the app.
  • Treating swipe-away as the same as system kill.
  • Believing foreground services/WorkManager prevent all kills (they lower the risk only).

notes.title: What survives process death (and what does not)
notes.html:
The idea (Q66). Anything in memory is gone: variables, singletons, ViewModels, static fields, in-memory caches, running coroutines. Only things written to disk or into the saved-state Bundle can come back.

Survives Does not survive
Intent extras of the root activity (re-delivered via getIntent()) ViewModel fields
onSaveInstanceState Bundle (small, parcelable) Singletons / object / static / companion state
SavedStateHandle values In-memory repository caches, StateFlow values
View state with ids (EditText text, scroll) Running threads, coroutines, timers, network calls
Fragment back stack, arguments, FragmentManager state Bound services / connections
Navigation back stack (destination ids and args) Listeners/callback registrations
Room/SQLite, DataStore, SharedPreferences, files Temp files in cache/ may be cleared when low on space
Task/back stack structure (the activity stack the system tracks) WeakReference / LruCache contents

Application re-creation and singletons (Q70, Q86). After a kill the system creates a new process and a new Application object, runs Application.onCreate (plus all ContentProvider.onCreate and App Startup initializers), and only then recreates the top activity with its saved Bundle: the activity restores without anyone navigating through the splash/login/DI initialisation path. Production incident pattern: a login/session token held in a singleton (SessionManager.token) or a lateinit var set by the splash screen is null after restore, so the restored CheckoutActivity throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException / NullPointerException / lateinit property user has not been initialized, appearing in Crashlytics for users who "returned after a long time", often on low-RAM devices, and never reproducible during dev. Fixes: initialise in Application.onCreate or lazily from durable storage (EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore), make every screen independent of "how did I get here", and test with process death.

Industry examples. Firebase Crashlytics reports these as crashes with Application having just started (custom key "time since process start"); Google's guidance "do not rely on app-start order"; Hilt scopes @Singleton objects to the Application, recreated on new process.

Everyday analogy. After a power cut a computer reboots: anything you did not save to the hard drive is gone, and the programs are started fresh, not from the middle.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming a ViewModel or singleton is still there.
  • Relying on a static isInitialized flag.
  • Initialising shared state only in the launcher activity.

notes.title: Simulating and testing process death
notes.html:
The idea (Q67, Q82). You cannot test process death by rotating the phone. You have to kill the process the way the system does, while keeping the saved state.

Recipes.

  1. Put the app in the background (Home button) so the activity is stopped and the Bundle saved; then adb shell am kill com.example.app. (am kill only kills processes in the background / "safe to kill"; adb shell kill <pid> or Force stop loses the saved state because it clears the task.) Reopen from Recents: the activity is recreated with savedInstanceState != null.
  2. Android Studio: Logcat's "Terminate Application" button is a force-stop (loses state); the "Run" vs "Apply Changes" differs. Use the am kill route.
  3. Developer options: Don't keep activities destroys each activity when you leave it, simulating activity destruction (state saved, onDestroy called) but NOT process death, so singletons survive, thus may miss bugs. Also Background process limit ("No background processes") makes most apps get killed immediately.
  4. Automated: ActivityScenario.recreate() simulates config change recreation; for process death use StateRestorationTester (Compose) or ActivityScenario.moveToState(State.DESTROYED) with saved bundle patterns; Espresso tests with adb shell am kill via UiAutomator; the androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-viewmodel-savedstate SavedStateHandle can be tested via SavedStateHandle(mapOf(...)); ComposeTestRule.StateRestorationTester for rememberSaveable; Maestro/Firebase Test Lab scripts run am kill between steps.

Post-incident review (Q82). A team shipped a refactor tested only by rotation; bug appeared only after kill. Add to the checklist: every screen's "kill and restore" test in CI (a single instrumented test that navigates 3 screens deep, kills, restores), enable "Don't keep activities" for the QA build/debug menu, add custom Crashlytics keys (restored_from_saved_state), and a lint/code review rule: any new field in an Activity/ViewModel must be classified as "saved", "re-derivable" or "lost acceptable".

Industry examples. Google's "Test your app for process death" guide, Airbnb and Square use "kill and restore" in their QA matrices; Marathon/Maestro flows in CI.

Everyday analogy. A fire drill: you only know the building is safe if you actually practise leaving, not by checking the doors are unlocked.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing "Don't keep activities" and claiming process death is covered.
  • Killing via Android Studio's stop button (that is a force-stop).
  • Forgetting to put the app in background before am kill.

notes.title: When onSaveInstanceState runs
notes.html:
The idea (Q68). onSaveInstanceState(outState) is the system asking: "if you are going to be killed or recreated, give me a small note to hand back later." It is not a "save" lifecycle event you call; it is a best-effort snapshot.

Timing by API level.

  • Before API 28 (Android 9): called before onStop (and possibly before onPause).
  • API 28+: called after onStop. This change means onStop is no longer "state not yet saved"; fragment transactions after onStop throw IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState.
  • Called when the activity may be destroyed for system reasons (config change, background), not when the user presses Back or finish().
  • Not guaranteed to be called at all in some cases (e.g., the activity is simply finished); and onRestoreInstanceState is called only if a Bundle exists (after onStart; onCreate receives the same Bundle).

What gets saved by super.onSaveInstanceState. The view hierarchy state (ids), window state, fragment manager state (android:support:fragments), the SavedStateRegistry contents (via SavedStateRegistryController.performSave, including ViewModel SavedStateHandle providers) and Activity Result registry state. Always call super (usually first) or you lose all of this.

Best practice. Save only small IDs/flags needed to rebuild (selected item id, current step, scroll position, query text), never large objects. Heavy or critical data goes to a database or DataStore as the user types, not in this callback. Do not do slow work here: it runs on the main thread during stop and can cause ANR-like delays.

Industry examples. Google Keep saves notes to a DB continuously and uses saved state only for UI position; Gmail compose saves drafts in the background and keeps cursor/selection in Bundle.

Everyday analogy. A sticky note on the fridge before leaving ("I was on page 42"), not the whole book.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking it runs when the user presses Back.
  • Expecting order "onSaveInstanceState before onStop" on all versions.
  • Forgetting super.onSaveInstanceState.
  • Treating it as a place to persist data.

notes.title: Bundle limits and TransactionTooLargeException
notes.html:
The idea (Q69, Q81). The saved-state Bundle is sent to the system process (ActivityTaskManager) over Binder, and the Binder transaction buffer is a shared 1 MB limit per process (BINDER_VM_SIZE = 1 MB minus a small overhead, shared by all in-flight transactions of the process). If your saved state is too large, the app crashes with android.os.TransactionTooLargeException, or on Android 7+ with RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048... bytes. It happens on onStop (API 28+) or onPause (older), i.e. when the user leaves the screen, often when saving a Bitmap, large lists, or a big API response in the Bundle.

Rules of thumb. Keep the total state well below ~100 to 200 KB (many teams enforce 50 KB per Activity). Remember the limit is shared across everything the process sends at that moment, plus Fragments' saved states, view hierarchy state (a RecyclerView with big adapter state or WebView state) and ViewPager pages all add to the same Parcel.

Diagnosis. Crashlytics shows TransactionTooLargeException with ActivityThread.performStopActivityInner / StopActivityItem; the tool TooLargeTool (Jake Wharton) logs the size of each key; Bundle.toString() and Parcel.obtain().dataSize() to measure in debug; Android Studio's Memory profiler doesn't show Binder buffer so rely on logging.

Fixes (cost/perf optimisation, Q81).

  1. Store IDs/keys, not objects: save orderId, re-load from Room/DataStore.
  2. Move big data to a file/DB and save the path or key.
  3. Keep derived data in a ViewModel (rotation) and regenerate after kill.
  4. Use SavedStateHandle for tiny values only; setSaveEnabled(false) for heavy views (WebView, maps, large RecyclerView state); write custom onSaveInstanceState that drops large parts.
  5. Compress with efficient types (IntArray rather than List<Parcelable>); avoid Serializable (large and slow); use @Parcelize.
  6. Watch for libraries storing images or ads in state.

Cost angle. A big Bundle also means slower stop (serialization on main thread, e.g., 8 ms vs 200 ms), more Binder pressure and slower restoration; reducing it improved ANR and startup metrics in many apps.

Industry examples. Facebook and Twitter engineering blogs on TransactionTooLargeException; Jake Wharton's TooLargeTool; Instagram stores media in files, passing URIs.

Everyday analogy. Posting a parcel through a small letterbox: a letter fits, a suitcase jams the door and everyone behind queues.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the limit is per-Bundle 1 MB (it is a shared per-process Binder buffer).
  • Passing Bitmaps or big lists via Intent extras and Bundle.
  • Thinking the crash is on save; it appears at stop time on the main thread.

notes.title: View state restoration
notes.html:
The idea (Q72). Android restores each View's own state (text in an EditText, checked state, scroll offset) automatically, if it can find the right view again. It finds it by the view's android:id.

Mechanism. Activity.onSaveInstanceState -> Window.saveHierarchyState() -> View.saveHierarchyState(SparseArray<Parcelable>) walks the tree, and for each view with an id and isSaveEnabled() calls dispatchSaveInstanceState -> onSaveInstanceState (returns a BaseSavedState). Results are stored as a SparseArray keyed by view id in the Bundle (android:viewHierarchyState). On restore, the new view tree (inflated in onCreate) matches by id.

Typical problems.

  • Missing or duplicate ids (include the same layout twice: both children share ids, states overwrite each other: use android:saveEnabled="false" or unique ids).
  • Custom views not implementing onSaveInstanceState.
  • Dynamically added views need the same id each time (View.generateViewId() yields different ids across runs; assign stable ids).
  • Adapter-backed lists restore scroll offsets before the data exists (RecyclerView StateRestorationPolicy).
  • TextWatcher re-triggering on restore with stale text.
  • Fragments: onViewStateRestored is the callback after restoration.
  • Compose: rememberSaveable replaces this (see below); LazyListState uses a Saver.

Industry examples. Search boxes in Google Maps and Amazon retain the typed query via EditText state; forms in banking apps re-fill via SavedStateHandle since passwords/PII must not be saved in the Bundle in plain text (use android:saveEnabled="false" or importantForAutofill flags on sensitive fields).

Everyday analogy. Name tags on lockers: the system returns your jacket only if the locker still has the same number.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting restoration for views without ids.
  • Saving passwords through EditText auto-restoration.
  • Using generateViewId() for views that need state restore.

notes.title: SavedStateRegistry, SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable
notes.html:
SavedStateRegistry (Q73). A per-owner (Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry) registry in androidx.savedstate that lets any component register a SavedStateProvider under a unique string key. When the owner's state is saved, the registry calls saveState() on each provider and puts the result in the Bundle; on creation, consumeRestoredStateForKey(key) returns that Bundle. The owner calls performRestore(savedInstanceState) in onCreate and performSave(outState) in onSaveInstanceState. Important: you must consume restored state in onCreate/before STARTED, and keys must be unique. The registry is the basis for everything: SavedStateHandle, Fragment state, Navigation, rememberSaveable (via SaveableStateRegistry), and registerForActivityResult.

SavedStateHandle (Q74). A key-value map given to a ViewModel (ViewModel(savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle)) which is persisted through the registry, so values survive process death. Obtained by by viewModels() automatically via SavedStateViewModelFactory (CreationExtras/@HiltViewModel with SavedStateHandle injection). It also carries navigation arguments (fragment/destination arguments are put in it).

@HiltViewModel
class SearchViewModel @Inject constructor(private val state: SavedStateHandle, repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    val query = state.getStateFlow("query", "")                 // survives process death
    fun onQuery(q: String) { state["query"] = q }
    val results = query.debounce(300).flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }.stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), emptyList())
}

Limits: values must be Bundle-compatible (Parcelable/Serializable/primitives); size counts against the same ~1 MB Binder budget; it is saved at the same time as onSaveInstanceState (so not instantly: an in-flight value set just before a kill is saved only if the stop happened); getLiveData/getStateFlow helpers keep UI in sync.

rememberSaveable (Q76). Compose's equivalent for composable local state: var text by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }. It stores values in the SaveableStateRegistry (backed by the Activity's SavedStateRegistry), surviving rotation and process death. Non-Bundle types need a Saver (listSaver, mapSaver, or @Parcelize). Use remember for derived, cheap, non-critical state; rememberSaveable for user input; hoist state to ViewModel+SavedStateHandle for business state.

Industry examples. Now in Android keeps selected topics in ViewModel with SavedStateHandle; Jetpack Navigation passes arguments through it; e-commerce checkout wizards (Flipkart, Amazon) save the current step.

Everyday analogy. A cloakroom with numbered tickets (keys): any guest (component) can hand over a coat (data) and get back exactly their own with the ticket.

Common interview traps.

  • Saving huge objects in SavedStateHandle.
  • Treating it as persistence (it is cleared if the user swipes away).
  • Using remember for user input and losing it on rotation.
  • Reading the restored state after onCreate (too late).

notes.title: ViewModel versus saved state versus persistence
notes.html:
The idea (Q75, Q89). Three tools for three kinds of survival. Pick by what must survive and how big it is.

Layer Survives rotation Survives process death Survives swipe-away/reinstall Size Use for
In-memory ViewModel field Yes No No Any Loaded lists, in-flight state, derived UI state
SavedStateHandle / Bundle / rememberSaveable Yes Yes No Small (KBs) Ids, selected tab, step, query, scroll
Room / DataStore / file / server Yes Yes Yes (except uninstall; server survives) Large Drafts, orders, user data, anything valuable

Rule. Save the minimum identifier to re-derive UI (orderId, step), persist the valuable user data durably as it changes, keep the loaded data in the ViewModel cache and re-fetch if missing.

Checkout state design (Q89). Trade-off: should a multi-step checkout (address -> payment -> review) survive a kill? Design: the cart and chosen address live in Room/server (source of truth); the current step and form fields in SavedStateHandle (non-sensitive only); payment instrument tokens re-fetched; never keep card numbers in the Bundle (PCI: Bundle is persisted in system_server memory and can appear in logs and backups); idempotency key for order submission stored durably so a retry after restore doesn't double-charge; on restore re-validate price and stock because they may have changed.

Industry examples. Uber stores trip state server-side so a kill doesn't lose the ride; Swiggy persists the cart on the backend; Gmail drafts autosave to local DB and server.

Everyday analogy. Brain (ViewModel) = short-term memory, sticky note (saved state) = reminder on the desk, notebook (database) = permanent record.

Common interview traps.

  • Using SavedStateHandle as a database.
  • Keeping everything in ViewModel and calling it "restored".
  • Saving sensitive data in the Bundle.
  • Not designing idempotency for resumed transactions.

notes.title: Restoring the back stack, fragments and the task
notes.html:
The idea (Q78, Q79, Q83). After process death, the system does not just restart your launcher activity. The task record (the stack of activities the user had) is kept by ActivityTaskManager in system_server along with each activity's saved Bundle (ActivityRecord). When the user returns via Recents or an icon, the system recreates only the top activity (the one the user was last on) in the new process and recreates the activities below lazily, only when the user presses Back to them. Each is created with its own savedInstanceState; the Intent that started it is also retained.

Consequences.

  • The top activity may start without any earlier activity having run (no splash, no login, no DI setup, no Application custom state). It must work from its own Intent + saved state.
  • The Navigation back stack is restored by NavController.restoreState: destinations and arguments are recreated from android:navigation:... saved state; NavBackStackEntry ViewModels are recreated empty (use SavedStateHandle); arguments must be Parcelable/serializable-safe; lambdas passed as arguments are lost.
  • Fragments (Q79): FragmentManager restores FragmentState for every fragment on the back stack, instantiating by class name via the FragmentFactory, with arguments; their views are only created for the visible one. Fragment fields and listeners are gone; fragments that rely on the parent activity having set a listener crash (ClassCastException/lateinit not initialised) after restoration. Dialog fragments reappear.
  • Launch mode/taskAffinity/clearTaskOnLaunch/alwaysRetainTaskState modify how the task is kept (clearTaskOnLaunch clears after a long absence, 30 min reset logic).
  • Android 12+ moved to "restore from the last-activity-in-task" with the splash screen API; Android 12 changed back button behaviour for root launcher activities (moves task to back rather than finishing), which interacts with restoring.

Industry examples. Deep checkout screens in Amazon/Flipkart restored directly; banking apps force re-authentication on restore, redirecting to a PIN screen before showing the restored page (via a base activity or an ActivityLifecycleCallbacks guard).

Everyday analogy. A bookmark in a book: when you reopen it, you land on that page directly without re-reading the chapters before.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming the launcher/splash always runs first.
  • Believing all activities in the task are recreated at once.
  • Passing non-parcelable arguments (lambdas) between destinations.
  • Fragment listener set via setListener after instantiation.

notes.title: Permission revocation and process death
notes.html:
The idea (Q84). If the user changes a runtime permission in Settings (revokes camera, location, or notifications) while your app is running, Android kills your app's process so the app can't continue with stale assumptions. When the user returns, the process restarts and the top activity is restored.

Consequences.

  • It is a process kill (not force-stop): the saved instance state is kept, so the activity is recreated with state.
  • Your code must never assume a permission granted earlier is still granted: check checkSelfPermission (or use ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission) at point of use, handle SecurityException, and re-ask with rationale (shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale). Auto-reset of permissions for unused apps (API 30+, "Remove permissions and free up space") also revokes permissions after months; Android 11+ one-time permissions are revoked when the app goes to background and the process is killed.
  • Restoration from a screen like "camera scanner" must handle "permission now missing" instead of crashing with SecurityException/black preview.
  • Apps in a multi-process setup handle onTrimMemory and ProcessLifecycleOwner do not see this.

Industry examples. Google Pay's QR scanner, Zoom's camera screens re-check the permission in onResume and show a "go to settings" CTA; Instagram's camera restores to the permission rationale screen.

Everyday analogy. A staff pass withdrawn while you're in the building: security walks you out and when you come back they check the pass again at the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Caching "permission granted" in a singleton or Preference.
  • Not rechecking in onResume after returning from Settings.
  • Assuming one-time permissions persist after backgrounding.

notes.title: Detecting process death in production
notes.html:
The idea (Q85). You can't catch the kill itself, but you can notice its effects on the next start and measure how often restoration happens.

Techniques.

  • ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(null, 0, 10) (API 30+): returns ApplicationExitInfo entries with reason codes (REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_CRASH, REASON_ANR, REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE, REASON_EXCESSIVE_RESOURCE_USAGE, REASON_SIGNALED, REASON_OTHER...), importance, pss, rss, and timestamp. Log these at next launch to analytics, which gives real rates of low-memory kills by device.
  • Restored-vs-fresh flag: in onCreate, savedInstanceState != null && <app singletons uninitialised / first activity since process start> = restored after process death. Mark isRestoredAfterProcessDeath in Firebase Analytics/Crashlytics custom keys: Crashlytics.setCustomKey("restored", true).
  • Process start time: Process.getStartElapsedRealtime() / ProcessLifecycleOwner ON_CREATE; a non-launcher activity as the first created one in a process means the user did not come through the launcher path.
  • onTrimMemory(level) callbacks (TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN, TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICAL, TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE) to flush caches and as a pressure signal. Android also provides MemoryInfo.lowMemory and getMyMemoryState.
  • Crash signatures: UninitializedPropertyAccessException, NullPointerException in activities with savedInstanceState != null.
  • Perfetto/Play Console Android vitals: "Excessive wakeups", "stuck partial wakelock", the "Low memory killer" metrics where available; device-level LMK stats via dumpsys meminfo, adb shell dumpsys activity processes.

Industry examples. Meta and Google Play Console use exit info to attribute background kills; Crashlytics adds device memory and ApplicationExitInfo data to reports.

Everyday analogy. Detecting that the lights went off while you were out: you cannot see it happen, but the clocks are blinking 12:00 when you return.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing there is a callback before the process is killed.
  • Treating onTrimMemory as a guarantee you will be killed.
  • Not recording the "restored" flag in crash reports.

notes.title: Process death incidents and design cases
notes.html:
Spot-the-bug (Q77). A form screen keeps private var draft: Draft? in the ViewModel, populated from a repository StateFlow; the user fills half of it, switches to a camera app, returns after the process was killed, and the form is blank, or the app crashes: viewModel.draft!! is null since the activity was recreated with the draftId in the saved state but the repository cache is empty. The reviewer should look for: fields only in ViewModel; singletons/lateinit; companion object state; non-Parcelable args; assumptions about navigation order; no savedInstanceState or SavedStateHandle. The fix: save draftId in SavedStateHandle, re-load draft from Room on init, persist text on change (debounced), null-safe UI.

Production incident (Q80). "Users report being logged out and a blank home screen after switching to UPI app and back" (low-end device, 3 GB RAM, 8% of sessions). Investigation: Application object restarted; the AuthRepository singleton stored the token in memory after login and didn't re-read from encrypted storage; restored HomeActivity ran with an empty session. Evidence: Crashlytics keys restored=true, ApplicationExitInfo.REASON_LOW_MEMORY spikes; reproduction with adb shell am kill. Fix: single source of truth in persisted storage, lazy by lazy read, idempotent init in Application.onCreate, an automated kill-and-restore test, and a breadcrumb event.

Migration at 10x scale (Q87). Moving from state-in-Activity/static to ViewModel + SavedStateHandle for 60 screens with 12M MAU: migrate screen by screen behind a flag; keep the old keys readable for one version (a restore of an old Bundle by a new app version after an update is possible: during an app update the process is killed and state may be restored into a new version, so changed keys/types can crash with ClassCastException/BadParcelableException: version your keys and wrap getParcelable in try/catch); track Bundle sizes (Bundle size budget per screen), restore success rate (restored sessions that reach the same screen without error), crash-free rate for savedInstanceState != null; stagger rollout 1% -> 10% -> 50%.

Android 14 restore bug (Q88). A known pattern (confirm against release notes for the exact build): on Android 14 (API 34) behaviour changes include stricter restrictions such as PendingIntent/intent-filter rules, and restored activities that start other activities from background or use implicit broadcasts can be blocked; also getParcelable(key) deprecated in favour of the typed getParcelable(key, Class) (API 33+). A typical bug presented is reading the saved Bundle with the wrong typed getter or class loader (BadParcelableException: ClassNotFoundException when unmarshalling) after restoration: ensure bundle.classLoader = javaClass.classLoader when reading custom Parcelables from a Bundle created elsewhere, and use BundleCompat.getParcelable(bundle, key, Type::class.java).

Resume where I left off (Q90, ambiguous requirement). Product says "when the user comes back the app should resume exactly where they left off." Clarify: after how long (a minute vs a day; the system itself may expire the task after ~30 minutes of inactivity depending on clearTaskOnLaunch/OEM), after swipe-away (system discards saved state, so durable persistence is needed), for sensitive screens (re-authenticate), for stale data (refresh prices), and for in-flight actions (payment: show status from server, never "resume" by re-submitting). Design: persist lastScreen + minimal params in DataStore on navigation; on cold start decide by age and sensitivity whether to deep-link there or go home; keep UI-only state in saved state.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant that must serve a returning customer their half-eaten order: it works if the waiter wrote the order on a pad (database), not if it was only remembered.

Common interview traps.

  • Fixing the symptom by ?: default values instead of persisting state.
  • Forgetting version skew in saved state after app updates.
  • Resuming payments by re-submitting.
  • Writing "resume exactly" without clarifying swipe-away and timeouts.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The OS kills background processes under memory pressure with no onDestroy; the task record and saved Bundle remain (system kill), but swipe-away and force-stop discard them.
  • On death: memory is lost (ViewModel, singletons, statics, caches, coroutines); disk, Bundle, SavedStateHandle and view state with ids survive.
  • After death a new Application starts and only the top activity is recreated, so screens must not depend on earlier screens' initialisation.
  • Test with adb shell am kill after backgrounding; "Don't keep activities" is not process death; automate kill-and-restore tests.
  • onSaveInstanceState runs before onStop pre-API 28 and after on 28+; keep it tiny; the Binder transaction buffer (about 1 MB shared) causes TransactionTooLargeException.
  • View state restores by unique id; SavedStateRegistry underlies SavedStateHandle, fragments, navigation and rememberSaveable.
  • Choose: ViewModel for loaded data, saved state for small ids/UI state, database/DataStore/server for valuable data; never put secrets in the Bundle.
  • Navigation and fragments restore by class name and arguments; listeners and lambdas do not survive.
  • Permission revocation kills the process; re-check permissions at use.
  • Detect in production with ApplicationExitInfo, a restored flag in Crashlytics and onTrimMemory.
  • Design "resume" features with persistence, clear expiry, re-authentication and idempotent actions.

questions.promptHtml: Why does Android kill app processes, and when does it happen? Does the user or the app get any warning?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every state-restoration bug starts from not believing the process can vanish silently. This checks the mental model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Android has finite RAM and no swap for app heaps, so it keeps apps as cached processes and kills the least important ones when memory is needed. The kill is by lmkd (low memory killer daemon) sending SIGKILL, so my code gets no callback, not even onDestroy. The user may also kill me (swipe from recents, force stop), and the system kills me for permission changes, crashes, and ANRs. A backgrounded app can be killed at any time, and when the user returns the system recreates the process and the top activity from saved state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Every process has an importance ranking computed by ActivityManager (the oom_adj / process state: foreground, visible, perceptible, service, cached). When free memory falls below pressure thresholds, lmkd (user space since Android 9, PSI based) kills cached processes first, least-recently-used and largest first, and only reaches visible or foreground processes in extreme cases.

Importance (high -> low)         Killed when
Foreground (resumed activity)    almost never (only OOM-level pressure)
Visible (paused, behind dialog)  very rare
Service (started FGS/service)    under pressure
Cached (stopped activities)      FIRST, any time, no warning

Kill reasons other than memory: user swipe/force stop, permission revoked from Settings (process killed so the new permission state is picked up), app crash, ANR, Process.killProcess, app update/reinstall, OEM battery managers (often more aggressive than AOSP, see the Doze/OEM chunk), and adb shell am kill.

What the app gets: onTrimMemory callbacks before cached processes die (levels like TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN, TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND), but these are hints, not guarantees. SIGKILL cannot be caught.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
none needed. Read the cause after the fact (API 30+):

val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(packageName, 0, 5).forEach {
    Log.d("Exit", "reason=${it.reason} importance=${it.importance} desc=${it.description}")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "onDestroy is called when the system kills the app." It is not; the process is gone.
  • Assuming a foreground service makes you unkillable. It only raises priority.
  • Believing that a user-visible app never dies. Visible processes are killed under extreme pressure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who does the killing in modern Android? → lmkd (native daemon), driven by kernel PSI memory-pressure signals; before Android 9 it was in-kernel lowmemorykiller.
  2. Is there a callback before kill? → No guaranteed one. onTrimMemory is advisory; onStop/onSaveInstanceState run when going to background, which is the real "last chance".
  3. How do you see why you were killed in production? → ApplicationExitInfo (API 30+), see the production-detection question below.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "low memory." The senior names who kills (lmkd), the ranking used (process state/oom_adj), that kills are uncatchable SIGKILL, and lists non-memory causes (permission revocation, OEM managers, user).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster appearing only on NullPointerException in activities that were backgrounded for a long time is almost always process death, not a logic bug.

questions.promptHtml: After the OS kills your process while the app is in the background, what survives and what is lost when the user comes back?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorized "use ViewModel" from those who can draw the boundary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Everything in the process memory is lost: statics, singletons, ViewModels, in-memory caches, running threads and coroutines. What survives is the Activity back stack records held in system_server, the saved-instance-state Bundle that I wrote in onSaveInstanceState for each activity, and anything on disk (files, SharedPreferences/DataStore, Room, account tokens in secure storage). The system recreates the process, runs Application.onCreate, and recreates the top activity with its Bundle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two stores live outside your process:

 App process (dies)                 system_server (survives)         Disk (survives)
 -----------------                  ------------------------         ---------------
 statics, singletons                Task/ActivityRecord stack        SharedPrefs, DataStore
 ViewModels, Repos' memory          saved Bundle per activity        Room, files, Keystore
 Threads, coroutines, Handlers      Intent that launched each        (survives unless app
 Fragment instances (rebuilt)       activity                         data cleared)
Item Config change Process death Back-press finish Swipe away
Static/singleton kept lost kept (process alive) usually lost
ViewModel kept lost cleared lost
Saved-state Bundle restored restored discarded discarded
Disk data kept kept kept kept
Activity Intent kept restored (same Intent) n/a n/a

The restored activity gets the original launch Intent back, so Intent extras are a (small) free persistence mechanism.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: none.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking ViewModel survives process death. It survives configuration changes only.
  • Putting user data only in a Repository MutableStateFlow held by a singleton.
  • Forgetting that a coroutine running in viewModelScope simply stops existing, with no cancellation callback executed in your code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the Bundle survive a device reboot? → No. It lives in system_server memory, not disk.
  2. Does the user's scroll position in a RecyclerView survive? → Yes if the view has an ID and the adapter data is available at restore time (see view-state question).
  3. Do the activities below the top one get recreated immediately? → No, lazily, when the user navigates back to them (see the system-restore question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists "ViewModel vs savedInstanceState." The senior draws the three stores (process, system_server, disk), notes the Intent is restored too, and calls out what is lost by non-obvious routes (coroutines, Handlers, in-flight network calls).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Upload progress kept only in a singleton disappeared after the user took a 20 minute phone call, because the process died while the app was cached.

questions.promptHtml: How do you reproduce process death locally? Is "Don't keep activities" enough?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many devs think they tested it when they did not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Don't keep activities" only destroys activities as I leave them; the process stays alive, so statics and singletons still hold their values and I miss the singleton bugs. For true process death I background the app (Home), then run adb shell am kill <package>, then reopen from Recents. am force-stop is not equivalent, because it also removes the saved state and the task.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Developer options > Don't keep activities: each activity is destroyed on stop, with onSaveInstanceState called and the state restored on return. It tests Bundle and ViewModel-less code paths, but the Application object and its statics survive.
  • adb shell am kill <pkg>: kills the app's background processes only if they are "safe to kill" (cached). If the app is in the foreground it does nothing. So press Home first. The task and saved state remain in system_server, so Recents shows the app and returning restores it. This is the faithful simulation.
  • adb shell am force-stop <pkg>: puts the package in the stopped state, removes its tasks/state; next launch is a fresh start. It tests cold start, not restoration.
  • Android Studio Logcat / "Terminate Application" and swipe from Recents: swipe from Recents removes the task, so state is discarded.
  • Background process limit (Developer options): limits cached processes, causing natural kills.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# 1. Open the app, navigate deep, then press Home
adb shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME
# 2. Kill like the OS would
adb shell am kill com.example.app
# 3. Verify process is gone
adb shell pidof com.example.app   # empty
# 4. Reopen from Recents (not from the launcher icon: launcher icon can start a new task state)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using force-stop and concluding "restore works" because the app opened fine.
  • Running am kill while the app is in the foreground and seeing nothing happen.
  • Launching from the launcher icon instead of Recents, which may deliver a fresh launch Intent rather than restoring the task. (Launcher normally brings the existing task to front, but with some launchers/flags behavior differs; Recents is the reliable path.)

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is "Don't keep activities" insufficient? → Process stays alive, so singletons/statics are not reset.
  2. Can you automate it? → Yes with UI Automator: press home, run am kill via UiDevice.executeShellCommand, relaunch from Recents. ActivityScenario.recreate() does not kill the process (see the testing scenario).
  3. Does the Bundle survive am kill? → Yes, it lives in system_server.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Don't keep activities." Senior: knows it is a different failure class, uses am kill after backgrounding, and distinguishes it from force-stop.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team shipped "tested" restoration with Don't Keep Activities on, yet a singleton token bug crashed 0.4% of sessions after backgrounding.

questions.promptHtml: When exactly is onSaveInstanceState called, and did that change across API levels? What are the cases where it is not called?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Saving at the wrong time is a classic source of lost state and IllegalStateException in fragment transactions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It is called when the system might need to recreate the activity later: when the activity goes to the background, or before a configuration-change recreation. Before API 28 it could run before or after onPause, but always before onStop. For apps targeting API 28+, it is called after onStop. It is not called when the user explicitly finishes the activity (back press, finish()), and it's not a lifecycle callback I can rely on for persistence.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the Activity docs: for apps targeting Android 9 (API 28) or higher, onSaveInstanceState is called after onStop; for older targets it could be called before onStop (and could be before or after onPause). I believe the switch is keyed on targetSdk, not just OS; verify on developer.android.com.

Why the change: the state Bundle is sent to system_server as part of the stop handshake (activityStopped(token, state, ...)). Moving the call after onStop means that state produced in onStop is captured, and fragment transactions committed after onSaveInstanceState throw IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState. The window for that bug changed with the order.

API < 28 target:  onPause -> onSaveInstanceState -> onStop
API >= 28 target: onPause -> onStop -> onSaveInstanceState

Not called when: finish() / back press (the user said "I'm done"), or when the process is killed without a stop path (crash, SIGKILL while foreground). It IS called on rotation and when another activity covers the whole screen. Not guaranteed to be called for an activity that is visible but unfocused (dialog/multi-window pause only).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState) // saves view hierarchy + fragments + SavedStateRegistry
    outState.putString(KEY_DRAFT, draft)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Omitting super.onSaveInstanceState: view state, fragments and SavedStateRegistry providers stop saving.
  • Persisting data (DB writes) in it. It may not run, so use onStop/onPause or save eagerly.
  • Committing fragment transactions from async callbacks (network, coroutines) that can arrive after the state was saved: that throws IllegalStateException unless the commit is lifecycle-gated.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why was the order changed in P? → So that state changes made in onStop are captured and the framework can send the state with the stop handshake.
  2. Is onRestoreInstanceState symmetrical? → Called after onStart only if the Bundle is non-null; onCreate receives the same Bundle.
  3. Does ViewModel's SavedStateHandle hook in here? → Yes, through the SavedStateRegistry provider "androidx.lifecycle.internal.SavedStateHandlesProvider" (see registry question).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "called before the activity may be destroyed." Senior: knows the API 28 ordering, what registers into it, and why it must not be used as a persistence hook.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An async callback committed a fragment after the app was stopped on Android 9+ devices and produced the notorious "after onSaveInstanceState" crash spike.

questions.promptHtml: What is the size limit on saved instance state, and what happens when you exceed it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding that the Bundle crosses Binder, and that the limit is shared and not per-Bundle.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The saved Bundle is sent to system_server over Binder, and Binder has a 1 MB transaction buffer shared by all in-flight transactions of the process. Overshoot and you get TransactionTooLargeException, which since Android 7 (API 24) crashes the app instead of being silently logged. In practice, I keep saved state to a few tens of KB, store ids and small state, and put big data on disk or in a repository.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The buffer is 1 MB - 8 KB of mmapped memory per process, shared between all simultaneous transactions. On the stop path, the saved state of the activity is part of a transaction; other pending transactions (e.g. startActivity with a large Intent, other calls) reduce what is available, so a 600 KB Bundle can fail on one device and pass on another. The exception can be thrown from onStop on Android N+ (the app crashes); on earlier versions it was logged and the state was lost.

Typical culprits: bitmaps in the Bundle, big lists of Parcelables (the Parcel overhead of each object and each field name key adds up), JSON strings, and a fragment-state explosion (many fragments each saving adapters/list state). The Bundle also includes automatic view state and FragmentManager state, not just yours.

Diagnosis: log bundle size by parceling it in debug builds; Android Studio and tools like "Bundle size" checks show it; the exception message often reads data parcel size 524288 bytes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// debug-only size probe
fun Bundle.sizeInBytes(): Int {
    val p = Parcel.obtain()
    return try { p.writeBundle(this); p.dataSize() } finally { p.recycle() }
}

override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) Log.d("State", "bundle=${outState.sizeInBytes()} B")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Limit is 1 MB per Bundle." It is shared across the process buffer, so you can fail well below 1 MB.
  • Catching the exception: it comes from the framework, not your code.
  • Saving full lists rather than IDs plus a reload path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What should I store instead? → The query/ID/filters/scroll key; reload from DB/network.
  2. Does Intent extras count? → Yes, same Binder buffer on startActivity.
  3. What does the Android docs suggest as an upper bound? → Keep it small; a rule of thumb used in Android docs/guides is on the order of 50 KB (verify), well below the hard cap.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "1 MB limit." Senior: shared buffer, N+ crash behavior, includes framework state, and gives the replacement strategy and a debug-size check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image-picker screen saved a decoded Bitmap for "preview restore"; on low-end devices a 12-megapixel photo caused a TransactionTooLarge crash on every background.

questions.promptHtml: After process death, what exactly runs when the user returns, and what does it mean for singletons, DI graphs and initialization order?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A Hilt/Koin/Dagger user must know the activity can be the entry point with no launcher flow before it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The system forks a new process, creates the Application, runs ContentProvider onCreate first and then Application.onCreate, then recreates the top activity with its saved Bundle. All singletons are rebuilt empty. So any state loaded by a splash or login flow is gone, and the restored activity is now the entry point; it must work without the earlier screens having run.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Order in a fresh process:

Zygote fork -> Application.attachBaseContext
            -> ContentProvider.onCreate (all, incl. androidx.startup)
            -> Application.onCreate
            -> Activity.onCreate(savedInstanceState != null)   <- restored, not launched via splash

Consequences:

  • DI graph is rebuilt; any @Singleton is a new object. In-memory caches, auth state, feature flags, "isLoggedIn" caches are all null.
  • The restored activity might be deep in the app (screen 5 of a flow) and run before any async init finished.
  • The same entry can happen via a push notification, a broadcast, or a service start, none of which touch your launcher activity.
  • Static lateinit var or object holders initialized in SplashActivity.onCreate are the textbook bug.

Rule: every screen must derive its dependencies from the Application-level graph, which initializes from disk synchronously or via a loading state, not from "somebody ran earlier."

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BUG: set only in login flow
object Session { lateinit var token: String }

// FIX: derive from persisted source on demand
class SessionRepo(private val store: TokenStore) {
    suspend fun token(): String? = store.read()   // DataStore / EncryptedFile
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Initializing the DI container in the launcher activity.
  • Heavy blocking work in Application.onCreate to "make sure" everything is ready (slows every cold start).
  • Assuming Application.onCreate runs only once per user session: it runs once per process, and a process can die any time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Application.onCreate run before Activity.onCreate always? → Yes, in the process that hosts the component. In a multi-process app each process gets its own Application instance (see the P2 chunk).
  2. How do you block rendering until async init finishes? → Show a loading state driven by a state holder; for the splash use the SplashScreen API setKeepOnScreenCondition.
  3. Do ContentProviders run before Application.onCreate? → Yes, which is why libraries initialize there, and why too many hurt startup.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "singletons reset." Senior: gives the exact order, the entry-point problem, and designs screens to be independently restorable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: NullPointerException: lateinit property token has not been initialized clustered on activities, reproduced only after backgrounding for hours.

questions.subtopic: Swipe-away vs system kill vs finish
questions.promptHtml: The user swiped the app away from Recents, versus the system killed the cached process. What is the difference for state, and what does the user expect?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ensures the candidate does not over-promise restoration or lose data in the wrong case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: System kill preserves the task and the saved-state Bundle, so the user returns to the same screen and my restore code must rebuild it. Swiping away removes the task and discards saved state, so the next launch is a fresh start and savedInstanceState is null. Back-pressing out of the root activity finishes it: no state saved, ViewModel cleared. So restoration is for the "I did not leave" case; things the user explicitly dismissed should reset.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
User/system action Task kept Bundle kept Process Next launch
Home, system kills cached process yes yes killed restore screen
Swipe from Recents removed discarded may be killed (OEM dependent; services keep it alive) fresh (savedInstanceState == null)
Back out of root activity (finish) activity finished none often kept cached fresh activity, ViewModel new
Settings > Force stop removed discarded killed, package stopped fresh; alarms/broadcast cancelled until user launches
Reboot task list may show, state is not restored lost n/a fresh

After swipe-away, whether the process dies is vendor-specific. A foreground service keeps the process alive after swipe on AOSP; some OEMs kill it anyway.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
none; contrast in your logs:

override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    Log.d("Launch", if (savedInstanceState == null) "fresh launch" else "restored")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Persisting "draft state" only to Bundle and expecting it to survive a swipe: use disk if the user would expect it.
  • Treating savedInstanceState != null as proof of process death; it is also non-null after a rotation. Add a process-fresh flag if needed.
  • Assuming force-stop is "just another kill": it also blocks broadcasts and alarms until relaunch.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you distinguish rotation from process death in onCreate? → Static/ViewModel flag: the ViewModel instance (or a static) is fresh when the process is new, while savedInstanceState != null.
  2. Does the system kill a process after the user swipes away? → Not guaranteed; OEM policy.
  3. What happens to a bound/foreground service on swipe-away? → The service continues on AOSP; onTaskRemoved is called for services with stopWithTask=false.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: only describes "kill." Senior separates system kill, swipe, force stop, finish and reboot, and matches product expectations to each.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Support tickets "my draft vanished" were swipe-away cases where drafts lived only in the Bundle; the fix was autosaving drafts to Room.

questions.promptHtml: Which UI state does Android restore automatically after recreation, and which does it not? Why do some EditTexts lose text?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know what the framework gives for free before writing manual code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On recreation, the framework saves and restores the state of Views that have a unique ID and implement state saving: EditText text, CheckBox, scroll positions of RecyclerView's layout manager, etc. It does not save state of Views without an ID, nor data held in my fields, ViewModel or adapter. Text is lost when the View has no ID, the same ID is used twice, or I overwrite it in onCreate with a default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity.onSaveInstanceState calls window.saveHierarchyState, which walks the View tree and calls dispatchSaveInstanceState on each view that has id != NO_ID. The result is a SparseArray<Parcelable> keyed by view ID inside the Bundle. On restore, after onCreate inflated views, onRestoreInstanceState (after onStart) pushes the states back by ID.

Traps follow directly:

  • Two views with the same ID (typical in included layouts or items in a list) overwrite each other's state.
  • EditText is freezesText = true by default; plain TextView is not, so it restores nothing unless android:freezesText="true".
  • Programmatically created Views without View.generateViewId()/an ID are not saved.
  • Setting text in onCreate from a ViewModel default before restoration is fine, but setting it in onStart/onResume overwrites what was restored.
  • RecyclerView layout manager state restore needs the adapter data to be present when restoring; with async-loaded data, use Adapter.StateRestorationPolicy.PREVENT_WHEN_EMPTY (RecyclerView 1.2+).
  • Compose has no View IDs; state is restored only for rememberSaveable (see Q076).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FeedAdapter : ListAdapter<Item, VH>(DIFF) {
    init {
        // restore scroll position only once data arrives
        stateRestorationPolicy = StateRestorationPolicy.PREVENT_WHEN_EMPTY
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reusing @+id/title in a repeated include.
  • Relying on automatic restore for custom Views without implementing onSaveInstanceState with a BaseSavedState.
  • Resetting UI from onResume each time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a RecyclerView sometimes jump to the top after restore? → Adapter was empty when the layout manager tried to restore; use the restoration policy.
  2. How would a custom View save state? → Override onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState using View.BaseSavedState.
  3. Is it restored on rotation too? → Yes, same mechanism.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Android restores text." Senior knows it is by ID, why it fails, and the adapter timing issue.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A form with an included "address" block twice lost the billing address on every rotation due to duplicate IDs.

questions.promptHtml: What is SavedStateRegistry and how does it relate to onSaveInstanceState? How would you plug your own component into it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows if you understand the machinery under SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SavedStateRegistry is an AndroidX owner-scoped registry (Activity, Fragment, NavBackStackEntry) that lets components contribute to the saved Bundle without overriding onSaveInstanceState. Components register a SavedStateProvider under a key; when the owner is saved, each provider's saveState() is collected into one Bundle. On recreation I call consumeRestoredStateForKey to get my part back. It is the base for SavedStateHandle and rememberSaveable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ComponentActivity implements SavedStateRegistryOwner. In its onCreate it calls savedStateRegistryController.performRestore(savedInstanceState) and in onSaveInstanceState calls performSave(outState). The registry stores a nested Bundle under a reserved key, with one sub-Bundle per registered key. Your component:

  1. Must register its provider early (before the owner saves; commonly in the init block or onCreate).
  2. Reads previous state with consumeRestoredStateForKey(key), which is available after performRestore (i.e., once the owner's lifecycle reaches CREATED; checking lifecycle.currentState.isAtLeast(CREATED)).
  3. Returns a Bundle in saveState().
Activity.onSaveInstanceState
   -> SavedStateRegistryController.performSave(outState)
        -> for each provider: provider.saveState() -> Bundle
   (androidx.lifecycle.internal.SavedStateHandlesProvider is one of them: it serializes ALL ViewModels' SavedStateHandles)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DraftController(owner: SavedStateRegistryOwner) : SavedStateRegistry.SavedStateProvider {
    var draft: String = ""
    init {
        val registry = owner.savedStateRegistry
        registry.registerSavedStateProvider("draft", this)
        owner.lifecycle.addObserver(LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
            if (event == Lifecycle.Event.ON_CREATE) {
                draft = registry.consumeRestoredStateForKey("draft")?.getString("d") ?: ""
            }
        })
    }
    override fun saveState() = bundleOf("d" to draft)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Registering the same key twice -> IllegalArgumentException.
  • Reading restored state before the owner restored (before CREATED).
  • Holding the Activity in a provider that outlives it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the registry survive config changes? → Yes via the same save/restore path; it is rebuilt from the Bundle, not from the in-memory object.
  2. How is it related to SavedStateHandle? → The ViewModel's handle is registered as a provider under the owner's registry.
  3. Where does Compose hook in? → rememberSaveable uses SaveableStateRegistry, bridged to SavedStateRegistry by DisposableSaveableStateRegistry in setContent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it's for ViewModel state." Senior explains owner, provider, consume and ordering rules, and the layers on top.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom player controller using static caches switched to a registry provider so seek position survived kill without new Activity code.

questions.promptHtml: How does SavedStateHandle work, what can you store in it, and how does it combine with ViewModel scope?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard answer for "survive process death in MVVM"; the depth shows in limits and plumbing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SavedStateHandle is a key-value map handed to the ViewModel that is backed by the owner's saved-state Bundle. The ViewModel itself dies with the process, but the handle's content is saved by the registry and handed to the recreated ViewModel. It stores Bundle-compatible types (primitives, String, Parcelable, Serializable, arrays...), so I keep small UI state like selected ID, query text, filter. Large data goes to disk.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When the ViewModel is created via the default factory (SavedStateViewModelFactory, used by by viewModels() when the constructor takes a SavedStateHandle), it receives a handle built from: the restored Bundle for that ViewModel, merged with the owner's default arguments (the Activity's Intent extras or the Fragment's arguments; for Navigation, the destination args).

process alive:   ViewModel (kept) ---- handle (in-memory map)
onSaveInstanceState:  handle.contents --> Bundle --> system_server
process death:   new process -> new ViewModel -> handle pre-filled from Bundle

APIs: handle["key"], handle.get<T>(), getLiveData(key), getStateFlow(key, initial) (lifecycle 2.3/2.4+; verify), setSavedStateProvider(key, provider) for non-Bundle types. Writing to a getStateFlow's MutableStateFlow-like via handle[key] = v updates the flow.

Also: when the handle is created lazily per ViewModel key, the handle is saved only if the ViewModel was created before onSaveInstanceState.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@HiltViewModel
class SearchViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: SearchRepo,
    private val handle: SavedStateHandle,
) : ViewModel() {
    val query: StateFlow<String> = handle.getStateFlow("query", "")
    fun onQuery(q: String) { handle["query"] = q }

    val results = query.debounce(300).flatMapLatest { repo.search(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Storing lists of domain objects or Bitmaps: bloats the Bundle (TransactionTooLarge).
  • Storing non-Bundle types (lambda, custom class not Parcelable): crash at save time.
  • Duplicating state: a separate MutableStateFlow and the handle diverge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it survive config change? → Yes (the ViewModel survives anyway); the handle also survives process death.
  2. What if a ViewModel is created after the Activity saved? → Its handle is not in that Bundle.
  3. How do you unit test it? → Construct SavedStateHandle(mapOf("query" to "x")) directly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use SavedStateHandle for process death." Senior knows the plumbing, defaults from args, size discipline, and testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Search screen state retained across kill, but a "results" list saved in the handle caused TransactionTooLarge for 1% of users; fix: save only the query.

questions.subtopic: ViewModel vs saved state vs persistence
questions.promptHtml: How do you decide where a piece of state lives: ViewModel, SavedStateHandle, or persistent storage?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A design-judgment question; the answer is a framework, not a single tool.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask what the user expects and what the cost to recompute is. UI-scoped, expensive-to-rebuild data that only needs to survive rotation (loaded lists, in-flight request) goes in the ViewModel. Small, user-input-driven UI state that must survive process death (selected tab, query, scroll key, form text) goes in SavedStateHandle. Anything the user would be upset to lose after a swipe-away, or that is the source of truth (drafts, cart, auth), goes to disk/server.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State Where Reason
Loaded list, network result ViewModel (backed by repo/cache) rebuildable; too big for Bundle
Selected item ID, filters, search text SavedStateHandle small, cheap, user-created
Text typed in form Views (auto) + SavedStateHandle needs to survive kill
Cart, draft message, unsent upload Room / DataStore must survive swipe-away and reboot
Auth token Keystore-backed encrypted storage security; loaded on demand
Ephemeral one-shot (snackbar) neither; model as state consumed avoid replay

Mental test: "if the user swipes the app away, does this need to still exist?" yes -> disk. "If the system kills it while backgrounded, must the same screen come back?" yes -> saved state. "Rotation only?" -> ViewModel.

survives:          rotation  process-death  swipe-away  reboot
ViewModel             yes        no            no         no
SavedStateHandle      yes        yes           no         no
Disk                  yes        yes           yes        yes

sections.label: Code
sections.html: none.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Everything in SavedStateHandle."
  • Keeping the source of truth in the ViewModel with no persistence.
  • Saving derived data instead of its inputs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you store for a paged list? → The query and the anchor key, not the pages; reload via Paging/remote mediator.
  2. Where does the auth token live? → Disk (encrypted); never in a Bundle.
  3. Is a single source of truth possible across all three? → Disk-first repositories exposing Flow; ViewModel holds only UI state projections.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: ViewModel + onSaveInstanceState. Senior gives a decision rule tied to user expectation and a survival matrix.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: E-commerce cart held in ViewModel survived rotation but vanished after process death; fixed by moving the cart to Room.

questions.promptHtml: How does rememberSaveable relate to process death, and when does it fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks continuity: Compose state restoration builds on the same SavedStateRegistry. (Compose rendering belongs to A3.)

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: remember is lost on recreation; rememberSaveable stores its value in the same saved-state Bundle, so it survives configuration change and process death. It requires the value to be Bundle-saveable (primitives, Parcelable, Serializable) or provided with a custom Saver. It is subject to the same size limits as onSaveInstanceState.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
setContent in ComponentActivity wires a SaveableStateRegistry to the owner's SavedStateRegistry (a provider keyed by something like the saveable registry). When the Activity saves, all rememberSaveable values present in composition are written (each via its Saver). On recreation, the first composition at each call site receives restored values, matched by key (the call-site position/key in the composition plus an auto key). Items removed from composition are not saved. LazyColumn items: use rememberSaveable inside items to keep per-item state while scrolled off (the lazy list uses a SaveableStateHolder).

Failure modes: saving a non-saveable type throws when saving; saving a large list; moving the call site around so keys shift; ViewModel-owned state is not saved (use SavedStateHandle there).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Filter() {
    var query by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }            // String: fine
    var sel by rememberSaveable(stateSaver = ItemSaver) { mutableStateOf(Item.None) }
}
val ItemSaver = Saver<Item, String>(save = { it.id }, restore = { Item.byId(it) })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it for big data.
  • Expecting it to persist when the user swipes away.
  • Capturing lambdas in the saved state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. rememberSaveable vs ViewModel state? → ViewModel for business/screen state with survival of rotation; rememberSaveable for local UI element state; both can coexist.
  2. What happens at process death for nav destinations? → Nav restores back stack; destination's rememberSaveable values are restored per entry.
  3. Custom class? → Saver, listSaver, mapSaver, or @Parcelize.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "like remember but survives rotation." Senior links it to the registry, process death, size cost and Saver choices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bottom sheet's open/closed state was remembered, so after process death users came back to the wrong sheet state.

questions.contextHtml:
Crashlytics: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property item has not been initialized at DetailViewModel.load. 0.7% of sessions, only on Android 11+ devices with 3 GB RAM, never in QA. The detail screen is opened from a list via startActivity.

class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: DetailViewModel by viewModels()
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (savedInstanceState == null) {
            vm.item = intent.getParcelableExtra("item")!!   // set once
        }
        vm.load()
    }
}

class DetailViewModel : ViewModel() {
    lateinit var item: Item
    fun load() { /* uses item.id */ }
}

Red herring: the team suspects a race with a background sync.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why QA misses it, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Null check the item" or "move init before load." Doesn't recognize that after process death savedInstanceState != null but the ViewModel is new and empty.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it only after backgrounding? (confirms process death). Is Item Parcelable and large? How is the Activity launched (deep link, notification)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: always read the item id from the Intent in the ViewModel, not gated by savedInstanceState.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) process death: new ViewModel + non-null Bundle skips the init; (b) race with sync, unlikely since the exception is "not initialized", not stale data; (c) launched via a path without the extra.
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce: open detail, Home, adb shell am kill, reopen from Recents. Crash reproduces. Logcat shows savedInstanceState != null and a new ViewModel.
  5. Root cause: The guard savedInstanceState == null conflates "first creation of the Activity" with "first creation of the ViewModel". They differ after process death (and ViewModel is not restored).
  6. Fix: short term: take the ID from the Intent every time. Long term: use SavedStateHandle, which is pre-filled with Intent extras.
class DetailViewModel(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: ItemRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val id: String = checkNotNull(handle["itemId"])  // extras are default args
    val item = repo.observe(id).stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Lazily, null)
}

Pass an ID, not the parcelable. 7. Prevention: a process-death test (UI Automator am kill), lint/review rule: "no state init gated by savedInstanceState," avoid lateinit in ViewModels. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not adding android:configChanges or largeHeap; they don't address it. Not passing whole objects through Intent (size, staleness).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the extra is a Parcelable the ViewModel must have? → Still fine via handle (Parcelable supported) but prefer an ID and re-query.
  • Why Android 11+ only? → Not the cause; it just correlates with devices where the system kills background processes quickly (RAM, OEM policy).
  • Would Hilt change anything? → @HiltViewModel provides the same SavedStateHandle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite retail app had a "load once" flag in onCreate; the flag was true after kill, so the detail page loaded nothing. Fixed in a day; the test took a week to build.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests null checks only.
  • Hire: identifies process death and fixes via Intent/handle.
  • Strong hire: also explains Bundle-vs-ViewModel lifetime mismatch, adds a kill-based test and guideline.

questions.promptHtml: After process death, how is the navigation back stack restored, and what is not restored?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps are Navigation-based; the question probes what a NavController serializes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The NavController saves its back stack as part of the saved-state Bundle: for each entry, the destination ID, arguments, and the entry's saved state. On recreation it restores the graph and the back stack, then re-instantiates only the visible destination; entries below are recreated when popped to. ViewModels scoped to a back stack entry are new, but their SavedStateHandle is restored. Large arguments and in-memory objects are not restored beyond what is in the Bundle.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
NavHostFragment stores NavController.saveState() in its saved state (View-based Navigation); in Navigation Compose, rememberNavController uses rememberSaveable with the NavController's saver. Each entry's arguments and its SavedStateRegistry content (including SavedStateHandle) are persisted. For NavBackStackEntry-scoped ViewModels (graph-scoped shared VMs), each is recreated with its handle.

What breaks: passing large objects as args (bundle size), dynamic graph modifications that are not re-applied after restore (graph is set in code with conditional logic), popUpTo with state saved via saveState=true for multiple back stacks (bottom navigation) is also restored. Deep link flows that rebuild the stack restored from a Bundle that conflicts with a new Intent: handleDeepLink guards by FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK/Intent consumption flag (KEY_DEEP_LINK_HANDLED) to avoid replaying deep link on every recreation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Navigation Compose: pass ids only
composable("detail/{id}", arguments = listOf(navArgument("id") { type = NavType.StringType })) { entry ->
    val vm: DetailViewModel = hiltViewModel()   // gets SavedStateHandle with "id"
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Parcelable args holding big lists.
  • Conditional graph construction (e.g., based on login status) that evaluates differently after restore.
  • Assuming a graph-scoped ViewModel keeps its in-memory state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fragments below the top: are they alive? → No; only the top destination's Fragment is resumed, others recreated on navigation back (fragment lifecycle details are in the Fragments chunk).
  2. Does a login gate break it? → Yes if restored destinations require a session not yet loaded; check on start and redirect.
  3. Does it survive reboot? → No.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Navigation handles it." Senior says what is serialized, the lazy entry recreation, and how session gates and large args break it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow restored into step 3 with a null cart after kill; the nav layer was right, the cart state was in memory only.

questions.promptHtml: What does the FragmentManager do on recreation after process death, and which Fragment mistakes only show up then?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Fragments are restored automatically, which causes duplicate fragments and constructor crashes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: During super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) of the FragmentActivity, the FragmentManager restores its saved state and re-instantiates every fragment by class name, through the FragmentFactory (default: the public no-arg constructor), and restores their arguments Bundle and their saved state. So fragments need a no-arg-constructible class, data passed through arguments, and the Activity must not add them again when savedInstanceState != null.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
