FragmentManager state (back stack, fragment tags, args, view state) is part of the Bundle. On restore:

Activity.onCreate -> super.onCreate(saved) -> FragmentManager.restoreSaveState
   -> FragmentFactory.instantiate(classLoader, className)   // reflection
   -> fragment.mArguments restored, fragment.onCreate(saved) ...
Activity.onCreate body runs -> if you add() again => DUPLICATE fragment

Typical process-death-only bugs:

  • Fragment with a constructor taking dependencies and no FragmentFactory set before super.onCreate: Fragment$InstantiationException: ... could not find Fragment constructor.
  • Adding the fragment unconditionally in onCreate -> two instances (overlapping UI).
  • Fragment fields (listeners set on the instance, callbacks set by the parent) are gone; the restored instance has no callback. Use the Fragment Result API or a shared ViewModel instead.
  • Fragments that depend on a ViewModel state not restored. Setting a custom FragmentFactory must happen before super.onCreate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    supportFragmentManager.fragmentFactory = AppFragmentFactory(deps) // before super
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    if (savedInstanceState == null) {
        supportFragmentManager.commit { replace(R.id.container, ListFragment::class.java, null) }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing data with setters (fragment.listener = this).
  • Using newInstance(item) that stores the object in a field, not in arguments.
  • Missing the savedInstanceState == null guard.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Fragment need a no-arg constructor? → Reflection-based restore; fragment factory is the supported alternative.
  2. Do child fragments get restored? → Yes, with the parent's childFragmentManager.
  3. Where did the listener go? → Gone with the process; re-attach in onAttach/onCreate or use result APIs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use newInstance with arguments." Senior covers FragmentFactory ordering, duplicates, listener loss, and how to test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Two overlapping home fragments appeared only for users returning after hours: unconditional add() in onCreate.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app with 400k DAU. Support receives "I open the app from the multitask view after lunch and see a blank white screen; sometimes it crashes." Crashlytics shows NullPointerException: Attempt to invoke virtual method 'java.util.List ... getArticles()' on a null object reference in ArticleListFragment.onViewCreated, 0.9% of sessions, bucketed mostly in "background duration > 30 min." Release 6 weeks ago replaced an object ArticleCache with a DI singleton. Logcat from a repro device:

I ActivityManager: Start proc 18231:com.news/u0a212 for top-resumed-activity
D MainActivity: onCreate saved=Bundle[{android:viewHierarchyState=..., androidx.lifecycle...}]
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NullPointerException ... ArticleListFragment.onViewCreated
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and fix. What do you tell the product manager?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add null checks and a retry button." Treats symptom; doesn't ask why the cache is null on a restored screen, and doesn't repro with a kill.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the pattern correlated with time in background (yes -> process kill)? Does it need the Home -> wait path (not a rotation)? Device RAM mix? Did the crash start with the 6-weeks-old release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side feature flag or hotfix: if the cache is empty, show a loading state and refetch; never dereference. Ship via staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) restored fragment reads a cache that was filled only by the splash/first screen; (b) fragment's args missing; (c) corrupted state or race with refresh job. Evidence (a): saved=Bundle present means restore; Start proc = new process.
  4. How I'd verify: adb shell am kill com.news after backgrounding, reopen from Recents. Check ApplicationExitInfo for REASON_LOW_MEMORY distribution; break the crash rate by getHistoricalProcessExitReasons.
  5. Root cause: The article data was populated by SplashActivity's fetch. After process death the restored MainActivity and fragment run without the splash, so the DI singleton is empty.
  6. Fix: short-term: null-safe UI with loading. Long-term: make the repository the owner of data: Room as the source of truth and Flow reads; fragment restores only a list key/scroll position and renders from the DB; fetch if stale.
class ArticleRepo(private val dao: ArticleDao, private val api: Api) {
    val articles: Flow<List<Article>> = dao.observeAll()
    suspend fun refresh() = dao.replaceAll(api.fetch())
}
  1. Prevention: instrumentation test with am kill on each top-level screen; lint review rule against singletons populated by launcher screens; add ApplicationExitInfo logging.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not forcing the restored task to go through the splash (feels broken); not android:clearTaskOnLaunch to hide it (discards the user's place).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the PM wants zero cold-start wait on restore? → Render from Room instantly, refresh in the background.
  • Does largeHeap help? → No; this is not an OOM.
  • How do you size the problem? → 0.9% of 400k DAU ≈ 3,600 users/day; check the kill share via exit reasons.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite media app removed an "eager preload" because it slowed startup; the preload had been masking a dependency on in-memory state that only process death exposed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: null checks only.
  • Hire: identifies process death and repros with am kill; fixes data source.
  • Strong hire: single source of truth, exit-reason telemetry, regression test, rollout plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-album app, 150k DAU. Crash cluster: RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1042136 bytes thrown from ActivityThread.performStopActivity, 1.8% of sessions on devices with 2-3 GB RAM, mostly after viewing big albums. The album screen code:

override fun onSaveInstanceState(outState: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(outState)
    outState.putParcelableArrayList("photos", ArrayList(photos)) // up to 2,000 Photo objects
    outState.putParcelable("selectedThumb", selectedBitmap)       // 600x600 Bitmap
}

Each Photo has id, uri, caption, exif map (about 400 B). Red herring: a recent Glide upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it crashing, how large is it, what do you change, and how do you stop it recurring?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Reduce the number of photos" or compress the Bitmap. Doesn't compute the size or question what belongs in the Bundle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the crash reproduce only at stop/background? Max album size? Is photo data re-derivable (yes, DB/MediaStore)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove both puts in a hotfix. If the screen already has an ID/query it can reload.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) list + Bitmap in Bundle exceed the 1 MB Binder buffer; (b) Fragment state adds more; (c) Glide: unrelated.
  4. How I'd verify (with math): Photos: 2,000 x ~400 B + keys/uri overhead ≈ 0.8 MB+. Bitmap 600x600x4 B = 1.44 MB uncompressed alone (compressed on parcel at least; Bitmap in Parcel writes raw pixel data via ashmem for large ones, but still exceeds budget). Measure with the Parcel size helper in debug; reproduce with a 2,000 item album.
  5. Root cause: the saved state is sent over Binder with a 1 MB shared buffer; the Bundle was not meant to hold data.
  6. Fix: short-term: delete the puts. Long-term: keep albumId and selectedPhotoId in SavedStateHandle; read the list from the DB/MediaStore; re-decode the thumbnail via Glide.
  7. Prevention: debug builds assert on outState size above 100 KB; Crashlytics custom key with bundle size; code review rule: "IDs in Bundle, data on disk."
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catching the exception (it's framework thrown); not writing the list to a static (lost on kill, leaks).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could a file-based approach work? → Yes: write to cache file and save the path, but the file may be cleared; just reload from source.
  • Why doesn't it crash on the dev Pixel? → Faster stop handshake and fewer concurrent transactions; also the dataset is smaller.
  • Will compressing help? → Marginal; fix the design.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite app's "restore everything" mandate saved a full feed; after raising the album limit in the backend, a crash cluster arrived on release day with no code change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only compresses.
  • Hire: moves to IDs and reloads.
  • Strong hire: computes sizes, adds guard rails and telemetry.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review after the blank-screen outage (see previous incident). The team claims: "We have a test suite with ActivityScenario.recreate() for every screen and it all passed." The incident only reproduced after real process death. The suite runs on emulators in CI, 1,400 UI tests, 42 minutes.
questions.promptHtml: Why did the tests pass, and what test strategy would have caught it without making CI unbearable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more tests." Doesn't differentiate recreation from process death.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What do the tests do between steps? Are fakes injected as singletons? How long is a full instrumented run?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a small P0 set of kill-and-restore tests for the top 6 screens.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) recreate() destroys and recreates the activity in the same process, so statics and DI singletons survive; (b) fake repositories re-seeded by test rules hide the missing data; (c) tests start at the launcher, so the restored-entry path is never taken.
  4. How I'd verify: Add Log of Process.myPid() before and after recreate(): same PID, proving no process death.
  5. Root cause: a test taxonomy gap. ActivityScenario.recreate() equals configuration-change recreation (state is saved and restored, ViewModels retained). It is not process death.
  6. Fix: three layers:
    • Unit: SavedStateHandle(mapOf(...)) for ViewModel logic; verify the restore path from the handle.
    • Compose/UI: StateRestorationTester.emulateSavedInstanceStateRestore() for rememberSaveable.
    • End-to-end: UI Automator test: open the screen, press Home, executeShellCommand("am kill <pkg>"), relaunch from Recents, assert.
val device = UiDevice.getInstance(InstrumentationRegistry.getInstrumentation())
device.pressHome()
device.executeShellCommand("am kill ${BuildConfig.APPLICATION_ID}")
device.pressRecentApps()   // then select the app card
  1. Prevention: nightly (not per-PR) kill suite; a per-screen checklist in PR template; Don't-keep-activities on a CI shard.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not running all 1,400 tests with kills; cost vs coverage. Not trusting emulator "recents" automation on every OEM image: pin one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can instrumentation tests run in the same process as the app being killed? → The test process is separate from the app under test only when using UI Automator with a separate test APK; with the standard instrumentation, the test runs inside the app process and killing it kills the test, so the shell kill must be done from a different process or via an orchestrator.
  • Is force-stop acceptable in the test? → No, it discards state.
  • Robolectric? → Does not model process death.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found only 3 of 40 screens survived a real kill; the "tested" label had been applied to rotation tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes recreate() is enough.
  • Hire: distinguishes and uses a kill-based test.
  • Strong hire: layered strategy with costs and CI placement; explains test-process caveat.

questions.subtopic: How the system restores a task
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what the system does when the user taps the app in Recents after the process was killed. Who holds what, and why are only some activities recreated?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: L3 depth: it checks for knowledge of system_server's role, not only app-side callbacks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The task and each ActivityRecord (component, Intent, state flags, saved Bundle) are kept in system_server, in ActivityTaskManager's root task hierarchy. When I return, the system sees the record's process is dead, starts a new process via Zygote, and asks the new ActivityThread to launch the top activity with the stored Bundle. Activities below it are not recreated until the user navigates back, at which point the same mechanism runs for each.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When an activity stops, ActivityThread calls onSaveInstanceState and sends the Bundle to ATMS in the stop handshake; ATMS stores it in the ActivityRecord (mIcicle/persistent state). When the process dies, the ActivityRecords stay, flagged as having no app thread (app == null). Return path:

Recents tap -> ATMS moves task to front -> top ActivityRecord has no process
  -> ActivityTaskSupervisor.startSpecificActivity
  -> AMS.startProcessLocked -> Zygote fork -> bindApplication (Application.onCreate)
  -> realStartActivityLocked -> LaunchActivityItem (Intent, savedState, ...)
  -> ActivityThread.performLaunchActivity -> Activity.onCreate(savedState)
Back pressed -> next record below: same path again (its own Bundle)

Notes:

  • The saved state is in system_server memory, not disk; system_server restart or reboot loses it (the recents list can persist, but the Bundle does not).
  • Persisted task metadata: Recents thumbnails and task descriptions are kept on disk.
  • If the Bundle is large, TransactionTooLarge hits on both the save and launch direction.
  • The activities that were never the top or were already finished have no records.
  • Multi-activity apps: each activity gets its own Bundle, so ordering between activities after restoration is lazy.

I am describing AOSP internals from memory; names such as ActivityTaskSupervisor changed across releases (e.g., ActivityStackSupervisor before Android 11/12), so be cautious quoting exact names in interviews.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
inspect it live:

adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -E "ActivityRecord|state=|app="
# after am kill: ActivityRecord remains, app=null / process not running

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the app "stores state in the system." It's system_server memory, bounded by the Binder size.
  • Assuming all activities restore at once.
  • Not considering that the entry Intent is also restored.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about launchMode=singleTask activities? → Same record logic; onNewIntent applies only for live instances.
  2. What if the activity finishes while backgrounded? → The record is removed; no restoration.
  3. Why does the restored activity not go through the launcher activity? → The task stack restores records, not the launch path.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Android calls onCreate with the Bundle." Senior explains system_server ownership, lazy restore of lower activities, and limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Debugging a bug appearing only in the second activity after kill: the lower activity was restored later, after a state singleton changed.

questions.promptHtml: What happens to your process if the user revokes a runtime permission in Settings while the app is in the background? How should your code handle the return?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Combines the platform behavior (kill) with a defensive restore design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The system kills the app's process when a runtime permission is revoked from Settings so the app doesn't keep running with the old grant; this is documented behavior. When the user returns, the process is recreated and the restored activity runs with the permission now missing. So I check permissions at the point of use every time, never assume that a restored screen still has what it had, and degrade or re-request.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In AOSP, revoking a permission (or an app-op change) calls killUid/kill for the package with a reason such as permission change; this is reported as ApplicationExitInfo.REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE (API 30+). Same for the auto-reset of permissions of unused apps (Android 11+, apps targeting API 30+, and backported to Android 6+ devices via Google Play services): it resets permissions silently, and the next launch runs with them missing.

So the restore path meets this combination:

  • savedInstanceState says "camera preview screen," so the restored Activity tries to open the camera in onCreate -> SecurityException.
  • A foreground service that used the location permission is also stopped.
  • Cached "permission granted" booleans (static or SharedPreferences) are stale.

Rules: query the permission with checkSelfPermission (or ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission) when needed; keep no permanent flag; handle shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale and the "don't ask again"-like state (API 30+: two denials block the dialog).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    if (ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
        showPermissionNeeded()      // do not open camera
    } else startCamera()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Checking once in onCreate of the first screen and caching.
  • Restoring straight into a screen that requires a permission without a guard.
  • Treating the crash as "kill", whereas the underlying bug is missing a re-check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you see this in telemetry? → ApplicationExitInfo.reason == REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE.
  2. Does revoking from the notification shade kill? → Revoking via system UI flows ends in the same revoke path; verify behavior per release.
  3. Does granting a permission kill the process? → Granting does not require a kill for runtime permissions; some special app-ops changes restart the app.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "request the permission before use." Senior knows revocation kills, how to detect it, and designs the restore path to re-check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scanner app crashed with SecurityException for users who toggled camera off in Settings and returned via Recents.

questions.promptHtml: How do you detect and measure process death in production, and tell it apart from a crash, an ANR, or the user's swipe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors instrument before they guess; this tests knowledge of ApplicationExitInfo and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On API 30+ I call ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons at startup to read why previous processes ended: REASON_LOW_MEMORY, REASON_USER_REQUESTED, REASON_CRASH, REASON_ANR, REASON_PERMISSION_CHANGE, and so on, plus the importance when it died. I report it as telemetry. To detect a restored launch inside a process, I combine savedInstanceState != null with a "fresh process" flag set in Application.onCreate. Below API 30, I can only infer it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(packageName, pid, maxNum) returns recent ApplicationExitInfo records (the system keeps a small ring, roughly the last 16 per package; verify). Fields: reason, status, importance (RunningAppProcessInfo.IMPORTANCE_* at death; IMPORTANCE_CACHED + REASON_LOW_MEMORY is classic background kill), pss/rss, timestamp, description, and processStateSummary (set with setProcessStateSummary(byte[]) to attach your own marker, e.g. current screen name). Also traceInputStream for ANR traces.

Fresh-process detection:

Application.onCreate:  ProcessMarker.fresh = true
First Activity.onCreate(saved):
   saved != null && ProcessMarker.fresh  -> process death restore
   saved != null && !fresh               -> config change / Don't keep activities
   saved == null                         -> new launch
   then ProcessMarker.fresh = false

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Application.onCreate (API 30+)
val am = getSystemService(ActivityManager::class.java)
am.setProcessStateSummary("screen=unknown".toByteArray())
am.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons(packageName, 0, 3).firstOrNull()?.let {
    analytics.log("prev_exit", mapOf(
        "reason" to it.reason, "importance" to it.importance,
        "screen" to it.processStateSummary?.decodeToString()))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the list is complete or unlimited; old entries are dropped.
  • Treating savedInstanceState != null alone as "process death".
  • Reporting from the main thread blocking cold start; do it lazily after first frame.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it include native crashes? → REASON_CRASH_NATIVE.
  2. Can I know the screen at death? → Keep it updated with setProcessStateSummary (small, use sparingly).
  3. What do you do with the data? → Dashboard restore-launch rate per screen and per RAM class, then target tests at screens with high rates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Crashlytics shows crashes." Senior measures non-crash kills too and makes restore a monitored path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Telemetry showed 11% of sessions on 2 GB devices were restore launches, which justified a funded investment in restoration tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app, 1.2M DAU. Crashlytics: IllegalStateException: No auth token thrown from TransferRepository.send, plus a spike of HTTP 401 on /accounts for users who return after long backgrounds. 0.6% of sessions. Code:

@Singleton
class AuthManager @Inject constructor(private val api: AuthApi) {
    @Volatile var token: String? = null   // set by LoginActivity after login
    fun requireToken() = token ?: error("No auth token")
}

Splash/login sets the token; MainActivity restores into the "Transfers" tab. Security team insists tokens must never be stored in plain SharedPreferences. Red herring: server-side token TTL was shortened to 15 minutes the same week.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, how do you fix it without weakening security, and how do you avoid logging users out?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Store the token in SharedPreferences." Violates the security rule and ignores refresh/expiry semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do crashes correlate with long background times? Do 401s correlate with TTL change? Is there a refresh token? Where is the refresh token stored today? Are crashes on restored launches only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make requireToken non-fatal: on null, route to a "re-authenticate" state (biometric or login) rather than throwing. Roll back the TTL change only if the refresh flow is broken.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) process death resets the singleton and the restored screen bypasses login; (b) TTL=15 min causes legitimate 401 refresh failures; (c) race between two requests refreshing concurrently. (a) explains No auth token; (b) explains 401s; both can coexist, so separate the two crash classes.
  4. How I'd verify: am kill repro; Crashlytics key "restored_launch" from the fresh-process flag; correlate 401 with token age on the server logs.
  5. Root cause: token lived only in process memory, and the restored entry path skipped the login gate. Separately, the shorter TTL surfaced a missing refresh flow.
  6. Fix: persist the refresh token encrypted: Android Keystore-backed key (AES/GCM) + encrypted DataStore/EncryptedFile (note Jetpack Security-crypto EncryptedSharedPreferences is deprecated; prefer Keystore + own wrapper or Tink; verify current guidance). On start, AuthManager loads lazily and exposes suspend fun token() that refreshes via an OkHttp Authenticator (single-flight with a mutex). Access token can stay in memory; null means "refresh now."
suspend fun token(): String = mutex.withLock {
    cached?.takeIf { !it.isExpiring() }?.value ?: refresh().also { cached = it }.value
}
  1. Prevention: a kill-and-restore test on every authenticated screen; Crashlytics restored_launch key; rule: no error() for missing session state; gate navigation by an AuthState flow, not by a flag set in a flow's earlier step.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not storing access tokens long-term; not disabling the session timeout; not forcing a re-login on every kill (users lose their place); ask whether biometric re-auth is required for sensitive actions after kill.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the keystore key is invalidated (new biometric enrolled)? → Treat as logged out; re-authenticate; don't crash.
  • Multi-process? → Each process builds its own AuthManager; use a shared store.
  • What about backup/restore? → Exclude tokens from auto-backup (android:fullBackupContent/data extraction rules).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite bank app shipped without a process death test; the first symptom was a 401 spike after a lunchtime peak, not a crash graph.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: plain prefs.
  • Hire: persists refresh token securely and gates on auth state.
  • Strong hire: single-flight refresh, security trade-offs, telemetry, test plan.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app currently saves screen state with a hand-rolled onSaveInstanceState (JSON strings of the form model, about 30 KB per screen). Leadership plans to grow flows 10x: multi-step listing creation with up to 40 fields per step and 12 photos. Today: 2M DAU, 0.05% TransactionTooLarge. You must migrate to SavedStateHandle plus persistence while shipping weekly, with 70% of sessions in the old version at any time, and Android 8-15 support. Existing sessions in the middle of a listing must not lose drafts across the app update.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan and execute the migration safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace everything with SavedStateHandle in one PR." Ignores size growth, draft survival and version coexistence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the user expect for drafts: survive swipe-away? Reboot? Server-side draft already? PII in the drafts? Backward compatibility of saved formats across app updates (the old process Bundle cannot survive an update because the update kills the app).
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for old state across updates: an app update kills the process, so Bundles do not cross versions. The cross-version concern is persisted data only.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (risks): (a) the size explosion once photos are included; (b) schema drift of persisted drafts; (c) double sources of truth during rollout; (d) restore of a half-migrated screen.
  4. How I'd verify: Debug bundle-size assertions, Perfetto not needed; run a staged rollout with metrics: restore-launch crash rate, draft loss reports, TransactionTooLarge count.
  5. Root cause (of the risk): Bundle is a transport for tiny UI state, not storage.
  6. Fix (plan):
    1. Draft entity in Room (draftId, step, JSON payload, updatedAt, schemaVersion), photos as URIs/files in app storage.
    2. Screen state in SavedStateHandle stores only draftId, current step, and focused field key.
    3. Autosave on edit with debounce (e.g., 500 ms) and on onStop.
    4. Dual-read for two releases: new code reads the Room draft; if absent and a legacy blob exists, import once. No dual writes of the same data.
    5. Remote config flag for kill switch; staged rollout 1%/10%/50%/100%.
  7. Prevention: schema versioning with migrations, tests for each migration, instrumentation am kill on every step, size assertion in debug.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not putting photos or Base64 in the handle; not letting autosave write on every keystroke; not syncing drafts to the server unless the product requires multi-device.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Disk full during autosave? → Surface a non-blocking warning; retain in-memory state.
  • GDPR delete? → Draft table must be purged on logout/delete account.
  • What about tablets with multiple windows (two listing flows)? → Key by draftId, not a singleton "current draft."

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team kept both formats alive indefinitely "just in case"; the dual path caused the one data loss bug that mattered.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps APIs without plan.
  • Hire: IDs in handle, drafts in Room.
  • Strong hire: staged rollout, import path, size guards, privacy handling.

questions.contextHtml:
After targeting API 34, a ride-hailing app sees a crash in MapActivity only after the device has been idle for hours: IllegalStateException: Trip not loaded (0.3% of 800k DAU). Reviewing:

class MapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val vm: TripViewModel by viewModels()
    private var receiver: BroadcastReceiver? = null

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        TripSession.current = intent.getParcelableExtra("trip")   // static holder
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_map)
    }

    override fun onStart() {
        super.onStart()
        receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
            override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { vm.onDriverUpdate(i) }
        }
        registerReceiver(receiver, IntentFilter("com.ride.DRIVER_UPDATE"))
    }
    override fun onStop() { unregisterReceiver(receiver); super.onStop() }
}
object TripSession { var current: Trip? = null }
// Logcat on affected devices:
// W/ActivityTaskManager: Process com.ride has died: cch+0 CEM
// E/AndroidRuntime: Caused by: SecurityException: ...: One of RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts

Red herring: the team blames the new Android 14 battery policy.
questions.promptHtml: List every bug you can find and prioritize them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Finds only the receiver flag. Misses the static holder reset and getParcelableExtra deprecation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there two separate crash signatures? (yes: Trip not loaded and SecurityException). Does Trip not loaded come from a restored launch?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the receiver registration with the exported flag; it is deterministic on targetSdk 34 for context-registered receivers for non-system broadcasts (the check applies to apps targeting U+; verify against the behavior-changes page).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) registerReceiver without a flag -> SecurityException on API 34 target (not process death related); (b) TripSession.current set in onCreate from the Intent: after process death intent is restored too, so the trip comes back, but a ViewModel or other code reading TripSession.current before onCreate (e.g., a service restarted first) sees null; (c) deprecated getParcelableExtra(String) unsafe with newer API, use getParcelableExtra(key, Trip::class.java) on 33+; (d) unregister in onStop when registration might have thrown leads to IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered.
  4. How I'd verify: Run on an API 34 emulator with targetSdk 34 to see the SecurityException; repro the null by am kill and starting via a different entry such as a notification that starts a service first.
  5. Root cause: two independent bugs plus a latent one: missing receiver export flag; global mutable state that is not part of restoration; and potentially mismatched register/unregister.
  6. Fix:
ContextCompat.registerReceiver(this, receiver, IntentFilter("com.ride.DRIVER_UPDATE"),
    ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED)
// state: pass tripId, let the ViewModel get it from SavedStateHandle
class TripViewModel(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: TripRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val trip = repo.observe(checkNotNull(handle.get<String>("tripId")))
}

Replace the static holder with the ViewModel or repository. Register/unregister in matching onStart/onStop via a lifecycle observer. 7. Prevention: targetSdk upgrade checklist (receivers, FGS types, intent changes), lint UnspecifiedRegisterReceiverFlag (exists), process-death test. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not exporting the receiver; not disabling the battery optimization story as a fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should this be a local broadcast? → Use a Flow/SharedFlow from a repository; in-app broadcasts are a smell. (LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated.)
  • Why "only after hours idle"? → Because the stale process death correlates with long idle; the SecurityException is independent and hits all users.
  • Would RECEIVER_EXPORTED be right for driver updates from the server? → No, pushes arrive via FCM, not broadcast.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team saw two crash signatures merged under one dashboard title; separating them halved the time to fix.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one bug only.
  • Hire: both bugs with fixes.
  • Strong hire: separates signatures, removes global state, discusses targetSdk process.

questions.contextHtml: Design state handling for a 4-step checkout (address -> shipping -> payment -> review) used by 600k DAU. Requirements: survive rotation and process death; user must not re-type an address; card number must never be stored on device by the app; the cart is server-owned; users often leave to a banking app for OTP (the app stays backgrounded 1-5 minutes, on 2-3 GB devices the process is killed in about 8% of those trips). Single-activity with Navigation.
questions.promptHtml: Where does each piece of state live, and how do you handle the OTP round-trip?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ViewModel plus onSaveInstanceState for everything." Puts card data in a Bundle (security) and ignores the server-owned data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the payment handled by an SDK (hosted fields) in another process/activity? How do we receive the OTP result: deep link, redirect, callback? PCI scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); start from the failure modes.
  3. Hypotheses (risks), ranked: (a) kill during OTP loses step and form data; (b) payment SDK callback arrives to a fresh process without a ViewModel; (c) saved state leaking sensitive data (Bundles can end up in logs, backups, or crash reports); (d) stale cart.
  4. How I'd verify: am kill during the OTP step with a debug build; verify saved Bundle contents with a debug dump; run security review for PII in saved state.
  5. Root cause: n/a. Principle: state ownership by durability and sensitivity.
  6. Design: | State | Owner | Why | |---|---|---| | Cart, order id | Server (re-fetched by orderId) | source of truth | | Current step, orderId | SavedStateHandle + nav args | tiny, restore position | | Address draft | Room (encrypted if policy requires) + debounce | user would be upset to retype | | Selected shipping option id | SavedStateHandle | small | | Card number/CVV | Never persisted by us; payment SDK hosted fields; token only | PCI | | Payment intent id / OTP pending | Persisted (DataStore) before leaving the app | callback must be resumable | OTP round-trip: before launching the banking app, persist paymentIntentId and step; on return (deep link/callback), the handler reads the persisted pending record, queries the server for payment status (idempotent), and navigates accordingly; it never relies on in-memory state.
  7. Prevention: idempotency keys on order submit; tests: kill during each step; bundle dump asserts no PII.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not using a retained static "CheckoutSession"; not saving card fields to SavedStateHandle even though it feels convenient: Bundles are visible in memory dumps and can be captured by some tooling.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User kills app while payment is pending? → Server is the truth; poll or push; the UI shows "verifying payment."
  • Back stack after payment success? → Clear checkout from stack with popUpTo/inclusive.
  • Is FLAG_SECURE relevant? → For payment screens, yes against screenshots/recents thumbnails, separate concern.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite shop double-charged after OTP return because the callback replayed on a restored activity and the order submit had no idempotency key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blanket Bundle approach.
  • Hire: tiered ownership with sensible persistence.
  • Strong hire: PCI-aware, idempotency, resumable callback, test plan.

questions.contextHtml: Product requirement from the PM: "The app should always resume exactly where the user left off." The app: a learning platform with video lessons (HLS), quizzes, notes editor, and a feed. 900k DAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM or less. No more detail given. You have two weeks.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into something buildable, and what is explicitly out of scope?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, I'll save everything." Doesn't negotiate semantics, ignores swipe-away, reboot, and security.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "left off" mean after swipe-away? After reboot? After 2 weeks? After 4 hours? Is it per device or per account (cross-device)? Which screens: all or key ones (video, quiz, notes)? Are there screens that must not resume (payment, login, exam in progress)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Establish a baseline: measure restore-launch rate and which screens users are on at kill (exit reasons plus screen summary).
  3. Hypotheses (candidate semantic levels): Level 1: system kill: restore same screen and in-screen position (SavedState). Level 2: user-initiated exits: resume media position and drafts (disk). Level 3: cross-device resume (server). Each costs differently.
  4. How I'd verify: Prototype video resume with ExoPlayer/Media3 position saved to DataStore on onStop/every N seconds; test with am kill and swipe-away.
  5. Root cause: n/a; the ambiguity is the problem.
  6. Proposal:
    • Level 1 (all screens): nav back stack, SavedStateHandle for UI selection, scroll key; reload content from cache.
    • Level 2 (video, notes, quiz progress): persist position/draft locally with debounce, resume on next open ("Continue watching").
    • Level 3 (later): server-side progress per account.
    • Explicitly out: exam sessions, payment, auth screens resume only to the last safe state.
  7. Prevention: a per-screen "restore contract" table (restores/does not/why), tests in CI, telemetry of restore success.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not resurrecting stale feed content as if fresh; not auto-playing audio on restore without user action; not storing media buffers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• PM insists on "exactly" for swipe-away? → Explain Android semantics: swipe-away is an explicit dismissal; we resume content progress, not the UI stack.
  • How do you handle a 2-week-old restore? → Time-to-live on resume points; show "continue?" prompt.
  • Privacy? → Notes drafts are user data: encrypt at rest or excluded from backup as policy dictates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped Level 2 first and learned that "Continue watching" satisfied 90% of the requirement the PM had.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the requirement as written.
  • Hire: clarifies levels and scopes.
  • Strong hire: proposes tiers, contracts, telemetry, explicit exclusions, negotiates with product.
